utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/1-AR73, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, and the case manager for the Prosecution is Ms. Erasmus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Goran Mikulicic, and I am representing the Defence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can the accused hear the proceedings in a language which he understands?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann, these are your appeals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are getting some interference. I wonder if that could be checked? There are two appeals. We have had a chance of reading the (interference) -- (Discussion off the record)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, apparently there is something wrong with the computer and it will require ten minutes to repair, so we will rise while that is done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/1-AR73, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we have the appearances, I would like, on behalf of the Chamber, to thank the staff who have made this move possible. We started an hour ago unsuccessfully in courtroom 1. They had to work very hard to get this court ready and to have done so within the time, so we are grateful for that. Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, and Ms. Erasmus is the case manager for the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Goran Mikulicic, and in this case, I represent the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I will ask the accused Mr. Aleksovski if he can hear again in a language which he understands.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, yes, I can hear you very well, and last time I forgot to tell you that I can also understand you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, this is your appeal. It consists of two matters. Both seem to be closely interrelated, and although it is a matter for you how you set about addressing us, it would seem sensible to deal with both matters together. We have read the papers; therefore, I think you could take it that we have the background, and we would be grateful for your main submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please. Your Honour, I indeed will not traverse our written submissions, but by doing that, I don't want to de-emphasise the importance that we place upon those submissions. Indeed, much of what I will say today will deal primarily with the appeal in relation to the first decision of their Honours of the 22nd of October, 1998 -- it will deal primarily with that -- and to a large extent, I will rely on our submissions in written form in relation to the second matter, the second appeal, if Your Honours please, although, of course, I am available at any stage to assist Your Honours with any matters that Your Honours may wish to cover. Your Honours, we say this is an important appeal because it touches upon issues which, in national jurisdictions, we take for granted and are well understood. But in my submission, it may not be so that it is so well understood in this jurisdiction. The two matters that I wish to take Your Honours to today and to dwell upon, if I might, are, firstly: What is the object and purpose of the criminal trial as we understand it in this jurisdiction? The second issue is: Does the fair trial, as is required by the Rules and the Statute, mean a fair trial for the International Community as represented by the Prosecutor as well as for the accused? Your Honours, if I was to suggest that a criminal trial is a search for the truth, you would probably not disagree with that at all. You would accept that. But if I were to say to you that the search for the truth supersedes all other aspects of the trial such as that it could be reduced to a shapeless and formless event with no specified or particular beginning or end, I suspect Your Honours would say that is not a criminal trial. If Your Honours please, Article 21, paragraph 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal advises us to ensure that the accused shall be presumed innocent until proven guilty according to the provisions of the Statute. That, Your Honours, is the beginning of an indication of the fact that a trial before this Tribunal is something in pursuit of the guilt or innocence of the accused. When it comes to the pursuit of the truth, there are other inquiries that we may all be familiar with. For example, you may have an inquest into the cause of death of an individual or into the causes of a fire. Now, that may be the pursuit of the truth of those issues, but the determination of that issue and the standard of evidence relied upon, the standard of truth, if I may call it, of that, may not and probably would not satisfy a criminal tribunal that the evidence proves the issue beyond a reasonable doubt in terms of who perpetrated the killing or who started the fire. By saying all this, Your Honours, I am not trying to imply for one moment that a conviction or an acquittal of an accused person should be based on anything other than the truth. Clearly, witnesses are admonished to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. So, obviously, the trial process is dependent upon the truth. However, the truth is a concept quite distinct, in my submission, from the notion of proof beyond reasonable doubt. The truth of a matter may be readily ascertained by reference to a number of sources, but none of these sources may either individually or collectively constitute proof beyond a reasonable doubt. In my submission, Your Honours, it is well accepted that the liberty of an individual is considered far too precious to be dependent upon what, in some circumstances, may be accepted as the truth. Conversely, absolute truth may be something which is beyond proof beyond a reasonable doubt and it may be beyond it because it is simply not humanly possible to acquire it. So, Your Honours, you may have a situation where you accept the truth of an assertion, let's say, for example, the temperature yesterday was 10 degrees. You don't need to inquire into it; you accept the truth of that. But if that assertion is the basis upon which somebody is to be found guilty and incarcerated, you may say that is not sufficient proof. Conversely, you may have a case where a crime is committed at a particular scene. There are no eyewitnesses to the event, and so all that you have to determine the issue is circumstantial evidence, such as that there is a bus ticket where the individual went to that place or that there is forensic evidence of cloth fibres or whatever. That may not be the absolute truth of the matter, but it may be a matter upon which you have to alternately rely and conclude that the issue is proved beyond reasonable doubt. Further, when we say we look at the pursuit of the truth as such, it means different things in different forums. Commissions of inquiry, for example, are often free to roam from one particular issue to another in order to come up with a conclusion and a determination of what they say is the truth of something that happened. That, Your Honours, is not something that we say is the sole basis of a criminal trial. Your Honours, if I may, I would like to take the Appeals Chamber to the first motion that was filed by the Defence when they sought to have the evidence of Admiral Domazet admitted. I have numbered a copy of this motion for easy reference. I don't know whether Your Honours have that, and I don't know whether the numbered copy has been given to my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May I take Your Honours firstly to the paragraph that I have numbered paragraph 11? It appears on the second page of the motion under the heading of "Discussion," if Your Honours please. There is a numbered paragraph there in the original text which is 3, but it is, in fact, my number 11. The assertion by the Defence there is: "The Defence considers the basic duty of the Trial Chamber is to establish the truth; therefore, there can be no restrictions of a formal nature with respect to the presentation and admittance of evidence." Your Honours, what are these restrictions of a formal nature that are being referred to? Well, we are not told by the Defence in their motion, but I think it is clearly obvious that it includes Rules such as Rule 85(A), Rule 85, paragraph (A). If Your Honours please, Rule 85(A), provides, among other things, that "evidence at the trial shall be presented in the following sequence," a not unremarkable provision, and then it sets out the various orders that follow from there. But this, Your Honours, could be seen as a restriction, particularly if you have closed your case and you want to put further evidence in, because Rule 85 instructs us that this order is the order that is to be followed unless, of course, it is in the interests of justice to do otherwise. Going back, if I may, Your Honours, to again the motion of the Defence filed on the 29th of September, 1998, and if I may refer Your Honours to the paragraph that I have numbered 12? Your Honours see there a reference to Rule 89 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and then going over the page to Rule 17, immediately above -- I'm sorry, I apologise. Paragraph 17, immediately above the heading "Conclusion," we see there the Defence submission: "Therefore, the Defence has the opinion, regardless of the completed procedure of presentation of evidence, that there are no formal or legal obstacles for the presentation of the expert testimony ..." Again, a reference to these formal or legal obstacles. Your Honours, we wouldn't call them "formal or legal obstacles" as such. I think we would prefer a more neutral term, such as "the rules that govern or determine the procedure of the trial." Your Honours, Article 20, paragraph 1 of the Statute of the Tribunal mandates that proceedings are to be conducted in accordance with the Rules. At a minimum, Your Honours, Rule 85, that I had taken you to a moment ago, the Rule that deals with the order of the proceedings, which applies unless it is in the interests of justice of the Trial Chamber to direct otherwise, is one such Rule. The evidence that was sought to be introduced here, the evidence that was introduced here of Admiral Domazet, is directed to determining whether or not, in 1993, in Central Bosnia, there existed a state of international armed conflict. The import of what the Defence is saying by these rather broad and sweeping submissions is that the pursuit of the truth of a matter transcends all other constraints or limitations that may be imposed by the Articles and Rules which would seek to govern the admissibility of the evidence. Your Honours may feel that it is perhaps somewhat against interest for the Prosecution to be making submissions of this sort because often the shoe is on the other foot: The Prosecution is trying to achieve the admission of evidence against objections by the Defence, that the admissibility offends some Article or Rule under the Statute or the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, but Your Honours I think will agree with me that the Prosecution has a greater interest in preserving the integrity of the proceedings and in ensuring that the Rules are followed. What the Defence, in our submission, doesn't see by their broad and sweeping assertions in this motion is that such a principle of an all-encompassing pursuit of the truth may impact upon the right of a fair trial. In other words, such a wide-ranging assertion may trump all of the fair trial guarantees that lie at the heart of the proceedings before this Tribunal. Your Honours, the learned authors of the text "Criminal Procedure," second edition, 1992, page 34, and I have copies of this which I could hand to Your Honours if it would be of assistance to you and to my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, which text is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is a text "Criminal Procedure," Your Honours, second edition, by LaFave and Israel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which jurisdiction does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is from the United States, Your Honour. I only really wish to go to a very small part of it to pick up a point that I wish to make on this, Your Honour. They say on page 34, the top of the second column, Your Honours, under Chapter 1, "An Overview": "While the discovery of the truth is a major goal of the criminal justice process, there exists other goals that clearly are truth-deflecting. Here we have such goals as respecting the value of human dignity." Your Honours, please, we find similar such rules in our Rules of Evidence and Procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I ask you this question: What do you get out of that quotation that is relevant to this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What I get out of it is this, Your Honours, that the Trial Chamber, when reaching its decision were, as we say it does, to accept the proposition put that the pursuit is an all encompassing principle that permits the abandonment, if I can call it that, of the order of the trial, and because it is the pursuit of the truth that, therefore, it should be admitted at any stage of the proceedings, then I'm saying that's not what the Rules of Evidence and Procedure of the Tribunal are about. And indeed, there are examples of Rules which specifically are directed, in my submission, against, perhaps, the pursuit of the truth. They put brakes on the pursuit of the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But, Mr. Niemann, the order in which evidence is to be presented is expressly stated to be subject to the interests of justice, and you can't elevate a Rule relating to the order in which evidence is to be given to some master which controls the whole proceedings. What you have to look at in every case is it in the interests of justice to vary that order? Would it not be quicker if we went to the first proposition that if the evidence was going to be given orally by the admiral, could you really have objected to it being led out of order if there was no issue taken at the trial that this was the first time that they had heard of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, where do we go to after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should explain what I'm endeavouring to do here. I'm trying to point to one instance of where I say the Trial Chamber has erred, and I think it's important to demonstrate where we say there has been an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, suppose for a moment, taking up that point, we accept that there is a purpose in the criminal process, for instance, the purpose is to ascertain whether the Prosecution has to proved that the accused has committed the offence beyond reasonable doubt, and that is sometimes described as a central purpose of the process. We also accept, of course that, we are governed by the Article to which you referred, that the proceedings are conducted in accordance with the Rules. Supposing for the moment that we accept all that, is your case this: That the Trial Chamber were wrong in admitting this evidence, first of all, because it was not admissible as evidence? I don't think you're submitting that, but I would like to hear your submissions on it. Secondly, are you submitting that it was out of order, and again, I don't think you're submitting that, in light of your previous answers, or are you submitting, essentially, that it was unfair to admit it at that stage, and in particular, it was unfair to admit it if you had no chance to rebut it? Now, I know I'm trying to put words into your mouth. It's not always easy to do it, but perhaps we could have your submission on those points. It might be helpful. I should have added, and I don't want to, of course, hurry you, but if possible, we wish to deal with this matter this morning. I know we've had an hour taken out by matters out of your control, but if possible, we would like to deal with it this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would well expect to conclude in ample time for my colleague to address Your Honours and the matter be concluded this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm not -- I will not be going into it in great detail any further at this point, but Your Honour has addressed to me some questions, and I don't know whether -- I will, perhaps, proceed to answer them in the course of my submissions, but I can give you short answers to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The mischief we see by permitting this evidence to be admitted in the way that it was -- firstly, I should withdraw that. We would argue that the transcript of the evidence of Admiral Domazet is not admissible under the Rules. That would be our first proposition. If we are wrong in that, then we would say that the Rules prescribed that we, the Prosecution, who represent the International Community, have rights, as does the Defence, and they are as prescribed under Rule 85. And we say that by changing the order of admission, on the assumption that we are wrong and that it is, in fact, evidence, that we have been deprived of what we say the Rules entitle us to, namely to cross-examine or to rebut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Could I just clear one matter up? At the time this was argued in the trial court, had the admiral been cross-examined in the other trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It isn't very clear from the transcript. So the tender was of his evidence and his cross-examination; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I recollect that he had been cross-examined. It was one of the points. While we're on that topic, in the case of the confidential witness whose evidence you were seeking to tender, he had been cross-examined extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed. Yes, Your Honour. Your Honours, just to conclude, if I may, on the point that I was making, and I am indeed conscious of the fact that Your Honours have requested me to move directly to those issues that we have discussed, but I would, if I may, simply like to draw Your Honours' attention to the decision of the Trial Chamber of the 22nd of October, 1998, particularly where Their Honours give reasons for their decision and they entitle it "Evaluation", and again I have numbered certain copies which perhaps may be handed to Your Honours for easy reference, because if I refer to the paragraph numbers it's perhaps easier. Very quickly, Your Honours, I just wanted to pick up that thing that I was making. Clearly, the Defence are entitled, within reason, to make whatever submissions they like, and that we wouldn't be here if they had done that and that was the end of the matter. The point we make is that we submit that a reading of the decision suggests that they actually picked up what the Defence were submitting in their motion, and I quickly draw Your Honours' attention to these matters. The paragraph that I've numbered paragraph 9 picks up paragraph 89, which was the paragraph referred to by the Defence and described by the Defence, if I may, as the enabling provision to allow this evidence to be admitted. In paragraph 11, they again pick up this theme that the ascertainment of the truth is an essential principle. I'm saying we're not quarrelling with that at all, but if it's an essential principle which overrides everything else and you that ahead of anything else in the Rules, yes, we do quarrel with it. We say that's wrong and they erred there, they shouldn't have done that. So we submit that having regard to these and other provisions in their decision, very quickly, that's what they -- we submit they have done, and in so doing they have erred. Your Honours, the Statute of the Tribunal, Article 15, gives to Your Honours the authority to draft the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and as we've mentioned earlier, Article 21 prescribes that the trial shall be conducted in accordance with those Rules. It's our submission, Your Honours, that if the Trial Chamber seeks to change the order of presentation of the evidence and thereby -- and seeks to change the order of presentation of the evidence, they must have regard, in our submission, to the interests of justice, the Rule requires that, but what interests of justice do they need to have regard to? Simply, the answer to that is: How does it affect the other side? Does it preclude the other side from aspects of the procedure which may be available to them which are deprived by that course? I wish to move on, if I may, to the second issue, and that is that the question of affording rights to one party or the other. It's probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson has a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I had wanted to have this clarification earlier. The evidence of the confidential witness that you are seeking to tender in rebuttal, was that by way of a transcript as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And a video, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While we're dealing with this, I don't want to lose sight of your submissions as to why you say the admiral's evidence in the form of a transcript and the video were not admissible, and one matter you can assist us with is this: When you say they're not admissible, is it because of the circumstances in which they were admitted, that is, late in the day and without your being able to cross-examine? Is that the point, as I understand it, from the grounds of appeal, or do you say that it wasn't admissible in the form in which it was admitted because the transcript are ordered to be admitted? The transcript and the video are surely hearsay evidence in this trial. They come in the form of a document of a witness who has not given evidence from the witness box or the witness stand, and, therefore, it must be hearsay evidence. And hearsay evidence has been said, in this Tribunal, on more than one occasion, to be admissible, and has not been the subject of appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't say that hearsay evidence is inadmissible, and that's not our position. We say that the basis of why this evidence of the transcript of the proceedings is inadmissible is because of the operation of, in particular, Rule 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But that's the very point that Judge May raises with you. This is not a witness -- it is not the testimony of a witness, it is a statement made by a person who is not a witness in these proceedings, made outside the Tribunal. It happens to have been made as a witness in another trial, and it happens to be under some form of oath and subject to some form of cross-examination, but it is not being admitted as the testimony of a witness, it is being admitted solely as a hearsay statement made by that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, with respect, Your Honours, I don't believe that's the interpretation that's appropriate to put on it, having regard to Rule 90. It's easy to say, "Oh, well, what we'll do here is we'll ignore Rule 90 and we'll deal with these cases, documentary cases." We're not offending Rule 90 because it's something other than testimony. That is not correct, You Honour. It is testimony, and that's what is sought to be put before the Chamber, testimony. Now, it's testimony in a written form, perhaps, but that is the very issue to which the Rule 90 is directed to. It's saying, if you want to put evidence of testimony of a witness before the Tribunal, do it orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That is so. That is what Rule 90 says, and surely the issue which you are raising is that Rule 90 should prevail, and that if you want to get this evidence in, then you have to apply Rule 90. What is being said is this: That what, in fact, happened was Rule 90 was not applied, that the Rule which allows relevant and probative evidence to be admitted was applied. Accordingly, this evidence was admitted by way of hearsay evidence in the form of a document, and indeed, if you look at the order which the Trial Chamber made, that, I suggest, is what they meant. They said the Trial Chamber admitted his testimony, was the word they used, but in fact, it was the transcript, including the video recording and exhibits, they said, as documentary evidence. I also have a note that you yourself when presented with the ruling orally, said that your understanding was that this was being admitted as an exhibit. In a sense, I think you were right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you were right. But the point is this: Whether it was right to admit the testimony in the form which they did, there was a power to do so. The evidence was admissible in this form. Whether it was right to admit it in the face of Rule 90(A), which provides for oral testimony, is surely a discretion for the Trial Chamber. No doubt it is a matter which we are going to have to decide on this appeal, whether Rule 90(A) should be applied, or whether the Trial Chamber had the power and exercised their discretion rightly in admitting the testimony in this form. Going on, if I may, just for one moment, because it applies to your appeal, the second part of your appeal, rather, because you made precisely the same application in relation to your confidential witness to have his transcript admitted, have the transcript of his evidence admitted once the other evidence had been admitted, and that, presumably, was a tit for tat, and no doubt you had it in mind that the transcript would be admitted as documentary evidence, as hearsay evidence. And just for one moment, just extending it beyond that, you have great experience, Mr. Niemann, in these trials. Have you come across a transcript being admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I haven't come across it in any other -- firstly, I haven't seen it at all, but secondly, the only area where we get close to it is under Rule 94, paragraph (B), where the evidence of a proceeding which has, I would submit, concluded, where the facts have been adjudicated, can come before -- you may apply to put before the Trial Chamber. In those circumstances you achieve an objective similar to this, but what we say is the danger of all this is, and why we say Rule 90 does prevail, and why we would say, in relation to the first appeal, that there was no power to admit it is because of two issues. One, once it's adjudicated and may be admitted under Rule 94, it achieves that ease and convenience of trial which may otherwise be sought but it is a question which has been adjudicated and decided upon, and there is a great deal of certainty, much more certainty than a transcript of a witness in another case which is not concluded. Now, in their decision Their Honours said words to the effect that the evidence of Admiral Domazet was of indisputable value. I don't wish to misquote Your Honours, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you checked the original French for that? I wondered whether they were merely saying anything more than indisputable relevance, because anything that has probative value or is capable of establishing a fact must be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It was an unfortunate expression at best, I agree, but do you think they were saying anything more than it was indisputably relevant because they went on to say the weight of the evidence is something we'll have to consider later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I must admit, Your Honours, I've addressed my mind only to what they have said in the English version of it, which I know was checked by the English Judge, and I assumed that as a consequence of that it correctly reflected what Their Honours had intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But the wording follows, the weight of this is something we have to determine later, tends to suggest they were not saying it is of indisputable probative value. They are really saying it was of indisputable relevance, which clearly it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I can't say one way or the other because I'm only left with the text of the decision, but it seems to me, Your Honours, that the danger of this evidence being admitted in the way that it was, at this particular stage in the proceedings, and having regard to the witness himself -- which I'll come back to in a moment -- is that it's entirely possible for the other Trial Chamber to reach a conclusion that this evidence is not reliable and cannot be relied upon and come to a completely different determination on it. And from my reading of the English version, which may be different from the French, and I can't assist Your Honours with that, but it seems to me that Their Honours have put great store in it and presumably would have put reliance upon it if they were to conclude that its value was indisputable. So, Your Honours, I would say that -- that Rule 90 directs itself to the question of ensuring reliability of evidence which the safest way to achieve that is by way of oral testimony where the witness is cross-examined, and within the text of the provision itself it provides for exceptions. There are other exceptions, but it provides for exceptions, and that is depositions or video-conference link, and uses terms such as exceptional circumstances. It goes beyond just interests of justice, it goes on to exceptional circumstances. Now, my submission, Your Honours, if this is thought to be a somewhat rigid construction of the Rules, then in my submission, in what way is it rigid? What it does is not preclude, for example, the dying declaration of a person, because that clearly could be admitted under Rule 89. Rule 90 addresses itself to living witnesses, people who can appear and testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The difficulty here is sometimes getting the witnesses here, having them available. This is not a national jurisdiction, and the danger of your position is this, that it is unduly rigid and doesn't allow the Trial Chambers the flexibility which perhaps they should have as benches of Judges in determining what evidence they should have before them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When Their Honours drafted the Rules, presumably that was a matter that crossed their minds, if my construction of Rule 90, paragraph 1 is right, because that is precisely why they made a provision for depositions to be taken, which could be taken in the field in front of a presiding officer, that is precisely why we have video conference link. In our submission, Your Honours, one of the great merits of the adversarial trial is that reaching the conclusion of whether or not the witness is telling the truth or not is the process of cross-examination, the process of perhaps being able to present evidence which would rebut what that witness has to say. These issues may or may not -- certainly cross-examination would not be permissible if we proceeded by way of a documentary trial. Your Honours, the point that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that to the list that you mentioned of exceptions, a deposition and a video conference link, there is also affidavit evidence which was recently added. Are you making the point that the Rules are exhaustive as to those exceptional situations?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is my point, Your Honours. Indeed, perhaps -- I am grateful to Your Honour for drawing my attention to Rule 94 because 94 bis was in operation at the time that Their Honours made their decision. I understand 94 bis has been part of the Rules since at least July last year, and it sets out and prescribes a way in which this matter could have been resolved. Now, Their Honours didn't turn to that at all, they didn't mention that at all, 94 bis, and in my submission, that would have been a way of directly dealing with it. Admittedly, Their Honours weren't confronted with precisely the same situation as is envisaged by Rule 94 bis because it wasn't a statement, I would submit it wasn't a statement, and so I think what 94 bis is talking about is an expert's statement which comes before the Chamber in this form and creates an opportunity to permit the Court and the parties to rely upon it in the absence of cross-examination or of calling a witness, and it specifically deals with it, and I submit that that is what should have happened. If the Defence wanted to get this before the Chamber, this is the course they should have taken. Now, obviously, we would have said, "Now we want to cross-examine," and I would have thought at that moment, having regard particularly to this witness, that the Trial Chamber would have permitted that or should have permitted it. It should have permitted it in the interests of justice at least. But that procedure wasn't followed. Your Honours, we say that the reason why Article 90(A) says what it says and why it provides only for the receipt of the evidence of a witness by way of oral testimony unless there are exceptional circumstances, and then, if there are exceptional circumstances, they are prescribed, we say that that is well-illustrated by this particular case why that is so. Your Honours, you have no doubt read the transcript of the testimony of Admiral Domazet. We say he was quite an unsatisfactory witness. He refused, on I think a number of occasions, to answer questions that were put to him. Be that as it may, this man is an active duty officer in the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia and was sent to the Tribunal by the government of Croatia. I would submit, Your Honours, that he is not exactly, by definition, the objective quintessential witness on which all and sundry can rely. He is not likely to come before this Tribunal and say that his republic, his government, was engaged in an act of aggression against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993. That would be extraordinary having regard to those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I expect that that was put to him, wasn't it? I haven't seen the testimony. I expect, when he was cross-examined, whoever was prosecuting put all that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not entirely because the cross-examination was limited and there was considerable objections raised. He came before the Chamber in very strange circumstances. A subpoena had been issued to the Republic of Croatia to present certain documentary evidence which -- and I don't want to go into a lot of detail about this -- but for a number of reasons, that evidence didn't come before the Chamber. So what happened was he was sent along in lieu thereof. Then, when it came to cross-examining him, not far into the cross-examination at all, he said, "Well, I can't answer that because that's a sort of matter of national interest." It sort of went from there and downhill from there, I would submit, and even questions put to him by the Chamber, if I remember rightly, were not answered. So he was a very unsatisfactory witness, Your Honours, and he came in circumstances which were not entirely satisfactory. We have to be realistic about this. Croatia has a vested interest in establishing that there was no international armed conflict. Your Honours don't have to think far to conclude that that is the case. I mean, apart from international condemnation which may follow, I mean, such things as war reparations and otherwise. So he came before the Chamber in circumstances where it was crying out for his cross-examination. In our submission, Your Honours, when Their Honours said, "Oh, well, the Prosecutor has had the right to cross-examine," well, in our submission, Your Honours, firstly, that is a misreading of Rule 95 in any event because, in our submission, Rule 95(B) provides examination-in-chief, cross-examination, re-examination shall be allowed "in each case." "In each case," Your Honours, doesn't mean in the case of Blaskic and that therefore the Prosecution is stopped from thereafter cross-examining. As Your Honours well know, these issues can vary and do vary from case to case, and it is quite impossible to simply say cross-examination on one instance should be sufficient forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the words "in each case" there means in each trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Surely it means in each case of evidence for the Prosecution, evidence for the Defence, et cetera. It couldn't really be interpreted any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, that is an interpretation that can be placed on it. I would have thought that it is equally open to the construction that these matters will be allowed in each case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All the Rules apply to each case, don't they, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, maybe not, Your Honours, which may be our problem here. So, Your Honours, we say that having regard to the fact that this witness clearly should have been made available so that he could be cross-examined, it was troubling, Your Honours, how the Trial Chamber were going to determine the weight of the evidence of this witness in circumstances where they weren't able to observe his demeanour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But they have the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They have the video, but they don't have the benefit of further cross-examination. I mean, in my respectful submission, it is not to the point to say, "Well, he was cross-examined. Look at that and you can make an assessment of his demeanour, and that's all you need to do." Because each case is different. There are issues that arise in different cases which need to be addressed in different cases, and a witness may not even touch upon a point in one case but it becomes a central issue in another case, and it may be much more important, that other point in the other case, or if he does touch upon it, it may be just a passing reference to it. The issue of demeanour is not determined as a general principle where you just simply say, "Well, I saw him on television. Therefore, I can make that judgement." The issue, in my respectful submission, of demeanour is determined on the basis of that but including his answers to various questions, important questions, in the context of the particular case, the particular case where those questions have become of great interest to the parties, and that is where the Trial Chamber sits and watches and observes the witness when confronted with those issues. In my submission, Your Honours, they are not common in all cases. It is our position, Your Honours, that clearly Rule 90 cannot be just brushed aside and given no effect, and that's what would happen. I mean, it is all very well to say, "Well, this is a document. Why can't it be admitted as a document under Rule 89?" Well, yes, it is a document, but it is not a document in the traditional sense; it is a means of getting around Rule 90, if you call it a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The transcript is only a record of what was said. What was said is what they were trying to get into evidence by way of a hearsay statement, so normally you would call a witness to say, "I heard Admiral Domazet say this." But if you have a transcript and everybody agrees it is an accurate record, then obviously efficiency, if nothing else, would determine that the document go in. But what is in evidence are the statements which he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: As hearsay statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. And there would be -- I mean, there may be circumstances, if what Your Honour is saying is, well, if he was dead and this was the only evidence we had available, that may be the only course open to us, so you might say to me, "Well, what's the difference? It's the same position." My answer to that is, yes, sometimes the justice of the situation requires evidence to go in in this way because of circumstances which are beyond our control, namely, the death of the witness. What I say to Your Honours is, it would be entirely possible for the witness to come before the Chamber and for the Defence, who want to present this witness, to say, "Well, we don't want to ask him any questions because we asked him all the questions and the transcript of those questions is here." Now, that's fine, if the Defence wants to deal with it that way. There may be no objection to that. There may be, I don't know, but there may be no objection to it. It might be a quick and efficient way of resolving it. But all of that assumes that the Prosecution -- or the other party, let's not just call it the Prosecution, whatever party it is -- is going to have the right to cross-examine and to put to the witness the various issues that the other party says is relevant to their case. In our submission, what the Trial Chamber has done is just ignored Rule 90 and gone ahead and said 89 permits us to do it, and in our submission, all this procedure is a means to getting around what is a rigid provision and a strict provision but an appropriate one. Your Honours are going to be, in many instances in these trials, you are going to be relying upon the uncorroborated testimony of a witness, an eyewitness to an event, which is going to be the only evidence upon which you can reach a conclusion of a most serious kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, the real thing you are saying is that in the circumstances of this case, they shouldn't have allowed in a hearsay statement, and if I may say so, your best point so far has been your allegation that you weren't permitted to cross-examine him properly in the other trial. Not one word of this appears in any of the submissions that were made to the Trial Chamber, and there was nothing said, because you said at the time that you didn't think that oral argument was necessary. So that none of this was put before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in our submission, which was written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. I've got it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- I believe we specifically said that Rule 90 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. You put the argument about Rule 90, but you never put the next stage, which I think you have come now to some sort of discretionary argument, that you should have been entitled to cross-examine him because you had not been permitted fully to cross-examine him in the other trial, and there is not one word of that put before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The right of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, not the right of cross-examination, the fact that you had not been permitted fully to cross-examine him at least on issues of credit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect I say, under paragraph 7, at the bottom of that paragraph, "Prosecution submits that the general provisions of 89 must yield to the specific provisions of Rule 90. If Rule 90 prevails and the transcript of the testimony of Admiral Domazet should not be introduced especially in circumstances where a party to the proceedings, in this case, informs the Chamber of its wish to cross-examine the witness pursuant to Rule 85(B)."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't tell them why you wanted to cross-examine him further because you say you hadn't been entitled or permitted to cross-examine him fully in the other trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's rather important, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, with respect, Your Honour, I think that it is a very onerous test to say that we should have set out in our motion all those matters which we wanted to cross-examine on, and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. Forget the technicalities that seem to have been introduced in this Tribunal by having a motion for everything. It is a matter that you could have brought to the attention of the Tribunal orally, could you not, as part of your submissions as to why they should not permit the evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't believe we were invited at any stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You said quite expressly, according to the transcript, you didn't want to orally address the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is because Their Honours had already made a ruling. I would have thought it impertinent to address them on the question once Their Honours had ruled the admission of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, could you just move on to this extent -- I mean, I think we have your submissions now about hearsay. One of the points is this, surely, that the hearsay rule was invented because of the difficulty for juries of assessing the evidence when they hadn't seen the witness and hadn't seen him cross-examined, but we are dealing here with professional Judges, as it is often pointed out. So that although an important factor, of course, it might not be quite as important as it would be with a jury, professional Judges having more experience of evaluating evidence and documents and the like. Going on from there, you didn't immediately seek to appeal that ruling, of course, historically, you waited and you put your own motion in to call the evidence in similar form, what I have referred to as "a tit for tat," that you had put your evidence before the Trial Chamber. If the Trial Chamber had accepted your motion, you presumably would have little to complain of or would certainly not have appealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That clearly is the way it is. Well then, given those circumstances, if the Trial Chamber had acceded to your motion, they would have been faced with the evidence of the two witnesses in documentary form: in transcript but also, of course, we must remind ourselves, video form, so they would have the chance to see the witness. The Defence, no doubt, will take the point that they couldn't cross-examine, and you would say, "Well, they were cross-examined," as you said in your motion, "for two or three days, that witness, during the trial, so he was extensively cross-examined." Is there anything in principle wrong with a Trial Chamber, given the amount of evidence that there is in these trials, a Trial Chamber dealing with the matter in the way which, had your motion been acceded to, would have been done here, that the Trial Chamber would have had both sets of evidence in this form? Would you make any complaint of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the position that we were in required us to take various steps having regard to the exigencies of the point of the trial. Our position, which we believe we initially made fairly clear was that, (a) this evidence shouldn't have been admitted and (b) the reason we didn't want it admitted is because we hadn't cross-examined. That was our initial position. The Trial Chamber ruled against us in relation to that. We were confronted with, having then pronounced the position on the law, which was obviously binding upon us, to which we had to deal with it as best we could, we believed that, having regard to the fact that we had reached the point where all the evidence had concluded, I think most of the evidence -- all aspects of the evidence had concluded and we were only waiting to deal with submissions, that we could live with a situation, if that was the state of the law, we could live with that provided we could put some evidence before the Chamber to rebut that evidence and to enable them to balance the issue in this way. It may seem that I am now here arguing against the position that we put and, in fact, I am. I make no bones about the fact that what we did was an expedient in order to bring about a conclusion of the matter. Our problems were greatly added to when we weren't even permitted to pursue that line, that is, attempt to rebut the evidence by way of alternative testimony. Our position is, Your Honours, that the evidence of this witness should not have been put before the Trial Chamber in this way; the witness should have been called and the opportunity to cross-examine the witness should have been made available. That indeed is still our position. As I said, if Your Honours are against us on that, we say then, if Your Honours say that the evidence is indeed admissible and properly admissible and that Rule 90, paragraph 1, has no application to evidence in this form, then we would submit, Your Honours, that the evidence of the confidential witness should then be admitted in like manner, which is exactly the same position now as what it was then. We haven't changed our position at all. In fact, we are on all fours with our original position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann (no interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm not receiving an interpretation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: I don't think we should go on further entering into detail. You can hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I can now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: I said that we would not prolong this discussion with the Trial Chamber because most of the arguments have been presented in written form. However, I feel that the question that was raised by the Presiding Judge, Judge May, is a very important one. As you told us at the beginning, that it is impossible, that is to say, that it is not legal to present the testimony before any other Trial Chamber, for example, in the Blaskic case, that is to say, that it cannot be presented to the Chamber concerning the Aleksovski trial and for reasons founded upon Article 90. A little while later, you yourself asked the Trial Chamber to hear testimony from a witness who was a confidential witness and you forgot the illegal character evoked previously. So there seems to be a slight contradiction in that regard, as regards your position, and I think that you are fully conscious of that. You cannot support one thing and the opposite as well. You cannot say that it is impossible in one case and then, without taking the necessary precautions, come and say that I would be satisfied and that it becomes legal if it is within the framework, falls within the framework of a certain form of equality between the two parties. Now, if I have understood you correctly, and everything that has been said takes on importance as far as you are concerned from the moment when the principle of the equality of the parties and equality of arms is respected, and it would be acceptable within the framework of Article 89, if I understand you correctly, and it is your request that a confidential witness was presented, and you are basing that on Article 89, are you not? My question is as follows: Is this request of having an equality of arms for the two parties, would you be satisfied on the basis of Article 89? Is your own request based on Article 89, and so the equality of parties and equality of arms would be based on Article 89? Is that correct, Mr. Niemann? That is my question to you because when you shift to another terrain, you mustn't forget your own basis. Thank you, Mr. Niemann, for giving us your clarifications. I think that we can advance in matters and in examining this appeal now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Does Your Honour want me to address Your Honour on that point or is Your Honour satisfied with what I have said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Can you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would Your Honour like me to address the point that you raised, or I just thought perhaps by what you concluded that Your Honour is satisfied by the point from what I said in my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: No, I'm not at all satisfied. I hope that you are going to give us, briefly, your position, to state your position to us briefly as regards the justification of bringing to this hearing the justification and the fact that you yourself have asked that a confidential witness and testimony by that witness -- by transcript and by video be taken into account by the Trial Chamber, testimony that was given in another case. So I'd like to know -- to hear your clarifications on that issue, what your basis is and the juridical foundations for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honours, what our position was was this: That when the issue first arose by motion of the Defence to admit the evidence of Admiral Domazet, the position taken by the Prosecution was that that evidence should not be admitted in that form and that we raised two objections to it. We raised Rule 90 and Rule -- that Rule 90 overruled or covered the issue and Rule 89 didn't apply. Secondly, that the Prosecution sought the right to cross-examine the witness. That was our position and, Your Honour, I still say it is our position, we haven't changed from that, but what position we may take on the law is not determinative of the matter. The position on the law is determined by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber said that the evidence was admissible under Rule 89, notwithstanding that it was contrary to the position that we had maintained. We were left with no option at that point but to comply with the law. We didn't agree with the law but we had no option; that was the law. So we immediately took steps to seek to follow the best course that we thought was available to us, and that was to put in evidence of rebuttal. Then we were denied that opportunity. Now, when we come before you now, our position is exactly the same. We say the evidence in the form of the transcript of Admiral Domazet should not be admitted, and that Your Honours should decide that it shouldn't have been admitted and that the Trial Chamber had erred when it did admit it. Now, Your Honours might well be against me on that, and Your Honours may find in a similar way to the Trial Chamber that it is admissible under Rule 89. It's not our position now. We say it is still not admissible, but Your Honours may say -- and if Your Honours say it again we must comply with the law. The fact that we have a view on the law is determinative of very little or nothing. Now, if Your Honours do decide it is admissible, we ask you to admit the evidence of the confidential witness to give us the opportunity to rebut it, because we then extend the principle that if it's admissible for the Defence it should be admissible for the Prosecution in like matter. So I hope that assists Your Honour with that issue. Before I conclude, Your Honours, we're not seeking to say that the evidence of Admiral Domazet should not come before the Trial Chamber. We're not saying that. If the Trial Chamber believes it would be assisted by the evidence, fine. What we're saying is that he should be called, certainly should be called. And when the Trial Chamber said, "Well, having regard to his position, there was difficulties in him coming here," and we have difficulty from our side understanding where it came from, because it doesn't appear to come from anything that any of the parties said at least, and I wouldn't think that Croatia would have any difficulty at all in making him available, I would think that it's in their interest to do so, so what our position is, Your Honours, is that we're saying that we don't -- we're not asking you to make a decision which would end up by the Trial Chamber not having access to this evidence if it believed it were appropriate to be admitted, we're simply asking that the matter go back to them, that they review the matter in light of our submission, and that is that Rule 90 precludes the tendering of evidence in this form, and that Admiral Domazet should be called, and that the case should be opened. We're not contesting the -- whether or not it's in the interests of justice to reopen the case. The position we take is that if the Trial Chamber believes this evidence would assist them in reaching a determination of the matter, then we're not going to be arguing they shouldn't have the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't quick enough on this. What you're asking us to do is to allow your motion, to allow your appeal, rather, and to remit to the Trial Chamber; is this right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On what basis are you asking us to remit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We're asking that the decision -- that the Trial Chamber erred when it admitted the evidence of Admiral Domazet in the way that it did, that the matter be remitted back to them to reconsider the matter, and that Admiral Domazet be called if Their Honours are minded to reopen the case to permit that to happen. And once he's called, all this after flows from that in terms of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: An appeal to this Chamber surely gives this Chamber the right, if it says the Trial Chamber was wrong, to substitute its own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course. I merely make this submission, because I was concerned that Your Honours may be concerned that the triers of fact believed that this was information that they appropriately required in order for them to make a determination on the issue, and the position of us, the Prosecution, was not to seek to deprive them of that opportunity should that be something that they require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And if we're against you on that, what would you ask us to do in respect of your second appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours are against us on the question of admissibility and that you say that Rule 90 doesn't preclude its admission and that it is admissible under Rule 89, we ask Your Honour that the evidence of the confidential witness be admitted, or alternatively, that the Prosecution be given an opportunity to rebut the evidence as is prescribed by Rule 85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I realise that in the course of a trial things develop that you don't anticipate, and that you shouldn't be punished sometimes for having failed to raise a matter to the Trial Chamber. Surely what you should have done here when the application by the Defence was made, was to say, at that stage, if the Trial Chamber is against me, then I want, as a condition of the indulgence being granted to the Defence, a similar indulgence being granted to the Prosecution so that we can tender the evidence in reply. That would then give the accused the opportunity of saying, "I'm not prepared to pay that price. We'll call Admiral Domazet." That's where it may get to here, may it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is a course that perhaps could have been open to us. The only thing I can say in our defence of that is that at one stage we sought that the Trial Chamber stay the proceedings pending this appeal, and at that stage we said, "Well, we won't delay it if our evidence can come in. If there is a concern about delay, the Defence can admit our evidence into the proceedings."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The point I'm trying to make is the accused should be given the option of saying, "If that's the condition being imposed upon on getting this evidence in this way, I don't want it, and I'll call the admiral and let them call their mystery witness in reply." And he may have to be given that choice here, may he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, presumably he would be given that choice if the matter was remitted back, because he could then, having regard -- should we be successful, having regard to what Your Honours might say of the matter, presumably that would be a consideration they would have to take into account. Now, that doesn't address the question of how the Trial Chamber may feel about it. The Trial Chamber may say, "Nevertheless, we want the information." Well, there's another Rule to deal with that. They can bring in evidence, assuming this is evidence they can properly receive, they can do it under other Rules with their own motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, in arguing the inadmissibility of the transcript, you have confined yourself to Rule 90, and I understand the relevance of Rule 90, but isn't it also important to point out that there are no other provisions in the rules for the admissibility of the transcript? Provisions have been made for affidavits, so I wondered whether you want to broaden your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm indebted, Your Honour. In the course of what I had intended to put, I was to say that. I have, I think, made the submission that as far as I can see from reading the Rules, Rule 90 is -- deals with what I say is witness testimony. Whether -- and I say it's artificial to convert that into written documentary form and say, "Well, that's something different." In my submission, it's the same thing, it's getting witness testimony before the court. I agree entirely with Your Honour. My research of the Rules, there is no other Rule apart from what is in Rule 94 bis and 94 ter, and I say that evidence of a like nature may ultimately be put before the Chamber under Rule 94, paragraph (B). The point I make is that if it's thought that I'm being rigid in the view that I take of Rule 90, I'm not, because in my submission, there's ample other opportunities, ample other ways to give evidence before the Chamber without necessarily having to ultimately be confronted with calling the witness. There are ways it can be done. But much of it has to be done having regard to the interests of the parties. And Your Honour is quite right, there is no other Rule that deals with transcript. There's Rules that deal with affidavits, there's Rules that deal with statements but there's no Rules that deal with transcript in this form. And the only one that comes close to it, in my submission, is Rule 94(B). Finally, Your Honour, before I sit down, I haven't addressed you on an aspect that was raised by the Defence in their appeal brief dealing with the fact that we are untimely in our appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's been ruled on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's my point, Your Honour, and I wasn't going to raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Yes. I am reminded of a question Your Honour raised a moment ago about has there ever been another case where transcript was tendered, and I understand in the case of Kovacevic, which didn't reach conclusion, but in that case the transcript of a witness Greta was tendered from the Tadic case. The Tadic case hadn't been concluded. And it follows the point. So I think I may have said that I didn't know of any and I didn't, to be honest, Your Honours, but that is apparently one case where it happened. I -- but on that occasion, I believe she testified, Your Honour, she actually came and testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I was on that case and I can remember that. She was cross-examined, of course, which is the point. Mr. Niemann, is there anything else? Thank you very much. It's now quarter to one, which means that we have been sitting for an hour and a half, which is the normal time for a break. We had been hoping, as I said, to finish this matter expeditiously this morning, because the Judges have other matters this afternoon. Mr. Mikulicic, how long do you think you might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honours, the Defence believes that we'll be much briefer than my learned colleague, Mr. Niemann. It is impossible for me to say right now how much time exactly I will need, but I hope to finish within 30 minutes. I hope that I will be able to articulate my position within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just going to have a word with the legal officer. I'm going to ask the legal officer if he would have a word with the interpreters to see if we can determine this matter. I understand the interpreters are in agreement. We're very grateful. Mr. Mikulicic, don't think that you are prescribed as to time, and if you find you want more than half an hour, we'll have to take a break. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I by no means think that I will be at any disadvantage because of the fact that I said that I -- it won't take me more than 30 minutes to express my position. As Defence counsel and as a lawyer, I have to say that I really enjoyed listening to this legal discussion which was initiated by my learned colleague, Mr. Niemann. However, I believe that at this level, solution need not be sought on the basis of the motion of the Prosecutor that was submitted in this case. The opinion of the Defence is that the solution of the issue that has been addressed by the Prosecutor in his submission lies in -- at a different level, belongs to a different area. I believe that we can all agree that the Trial Chamber in the Aleksovski case has admitted the testimony of Admiral Domazet as documentary evidence. What does it mean actually? It means that the key argument of the Prosecutor, namely that he has been deprived of his right to cross-examination, is simply not relevant, and it is not relevant for an obvious reason, the fact that Defence had no opportunity to subject the witness to direct-examination. We believe that the Prosecution is not at a disadvantage and that the Defence is not at any disadvantage either. The equality of arms, the balance of equality, has been safeguarded. The Defence has suggested and the Trial Chamber accepted that in their decision, that the testimony of Admiral Domazet be admitted as transcript, that is as documentary evidence, by invoking Rule 39(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the International Tribunal, and that, I believe, is the essential issue here which should serve as the basis for the final decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take it you mean 89(C). It seems to have been translated as 39(C).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, 89, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the issues that have been raised by the Prosecutor today before this Honourable Appeals Chamber are the issues which go to the credibility of the testimony of Admiral Domazet. And I believe that at this particular moment and at this particular instance, one need not discuss the issue any further, because at this moment we don't know what importance, what weight the Trial Chamber is going to ascribe to the testimony of Admiral Domazet, the Trial Chamber that is in charge of the Aleksovski case. We'll know that only at the moment when final decision is reached by the Trial Chamber. In that decision, the Trial Chamber will state its opinion. They will evaluate the testimony of Admiral Domazet as, for example, crucial, and then after that the affected party can challenge the position of the Trial Chamber in their subsequent appeal. The Defence, therefore, believes that at this moment this issue cannot be discussed. My learned colleague, Mr. Niemann, has said that the Trial Chamber, by reaching its decision on the admission of the testimony of Admiral Domazet in the Aleksovski case, that the Trial Chamber has prejudged the case itself by stating that testimony of the said witness was indisputable. We do not wish to go any further into that and discuss the French original of the text and the English translation of the decision. However, we believe that the expression that was used in the English translation has to be understood in the context of the application of Rule 89(C). The Trial Chamber, by applying that Rule, has indicated that that particular piece of evidence might have some probative value, and that is what is at issue here. This goes to the very principle of admitting into evidence testimony from some other cases, and this decision has to be considered in that particular context. Whether this documentary evidence that was admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber in the Aleksovski case is of any relevant value or not can only be seen it at the conclusion of the case and in a possible appeal to the judgement. Such an appeal can, by all means, challenge the decision of the Trial Chamber, if that decision was so decisive as to influence the final judgement of the Trial Chamber, and that is the essence of the problem in the opinion of the Defence. We, therefore, believe that the Trial Chamber had absolute right to admit the testimony of Admiral Domazet into the evidence as documentary evidence by invoking Rule 89(C). It is a general power of the trial Chamber, and that Rule allows the Trial Chamber to admit as evidence any relevant piece of evidence that has some probative value. That concludes my first point. As regards the second part of the Prosecutor's appeal -- or, rather, the second appeal, that is the appeal to the decision of the Trial Chamber by which the Chamber rejected the Prosecutor's request to admit into evidence testimony of a confidential witness which was given in a closed session, the Defence believes that in that case too, the Trial Chamber has reached a legally justified decision. Let me articulate this. If we agree with the statement that the Trial Chamber is in charge of conducting proceedings, and that the trial proceedings are in the hands of the Trial Chamber in all aspects and that the Trial Chamber can govern the procedure of the said proceedings and issue all appropriate decisions, so if we agree with that, we then have to emphasise the fact that in the proceedings which are currently being conducted against General Blaskic before this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber in charge of that proceeding reached a decision regarding a closed session during which the confidential witness whose testimony is sought by the Prosecutor, that that witness gave his testimony in a closed session. Therefore, such a testimony is confidential by its nature and it cannot be accessible to anyone other than the parties involved in the said case. It is, therefore, inaccessible to the Trial Chamber sitting in the Aleksovski case as well. The Prosecutor is now suggesting that the transcript be admitted into evidence, the transcript that is covered by confidentiality measures. We are faced with at least two problems here. The first one, which consists in the fact that the Trial Chamber, which is supposed to admit that testimony in the sense of a Rule 89(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, must, as an conditio sine qua non, verify and check whether that particular piece of evidence has any probative value. It is very difficult for a Trial Chamber to evaluate probative evidence of a particular testimony when it does not have the right to inspect the said testimony. That's the first problem. The second one is, and the Defence believes that this particular problem should have been relevant for the appeal of the Prosecutor, is the fact that the Trial Chamber, which reached a decision on the confidentiality measures for the said witness, should have been requested to allow one particular testimony to be given access by parties in another case. I hope we can agree with the fact that one Trial Chamber does not have the power to alter, to change or in any other way influence the decisions of another Trial Chamber, and this is precisely what would happen if the request of the Prosecutor in the Aleksovski case were to be -- if the request was granted. Such an authorisation does not lie upon the Trial Chamber, and that is exactly the reason why the Prosecutor's motion should have been rejected as it indeed was by the Trial Chamber's decision. Your Honours, we're not dealing here with any infringement of -- or upsetting the equality of balance of the parties at the proceeding. We are dealing with issues that are of a procedural nature, and the Defence firmly believes, of course, that the procedure should be respected. If in the course of the proceedings there should arise certain disputable issues as regards the application of that procedure, each party to the proceeding has the possibility, has the right, to react to certain infringements or violations of the procedure. I will not take any more of your time, Your Honours, and let me conclude with a proposal. We propose that both -- we move that both motions by the Prosecutor be rejected and that the proceedings against Mr. Aleksovski be brought to an end. If I can be of any assistance to you, it will be my pleasure to help you with any explanations I can offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Mikulicic. There is one matter which I want your assistance, please, and that concerns the question of the Rules about confidentiality. Your submission is that the Aleksovski Trial Chamber could not make any order respecting a witness on about how protective measures had been imposed by the Blaskic Trial Chamber, and, therefore, the motion should have been rejected. Is there any reason why we shouldn't, as an Appeal Chamber, make some orders in respect of those protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence, with all due respect to the Trial Chamber, does not consider that the trial -- that the Appeals Chamber has that competency. The only Chamber that has the authorisation and competency to do this is the one which is in charge of the proceedings, and it is the view of the Defence counsel that the Trial Chamber should, in that particular case, should make the pertinent decisions. Of course, these decisions can be good ones, bad ones, legal, not legal or any other kind, but they are subject to appeal. Then the Appeals Chamber are able to decide whether the decisions were good ones or not, whether they were legally founded or not. But for as long as the proceeding is ongoing, and for as long as the competent Trial Chamber is in charge of those proceedings, the Defence counsel feels that that is the sole Chamber which is sovereign to make decisions in the case it is presiding over and nobody else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's assume that the other Trial Chamber does make an order giving you access to the evidence of this confidential witness. What would you say if the application had proceeded before the Trial Chamber in Aleksovski, and the Trial Chamber there had said to you, "Well, you are seeking a favour, an indulgence, because you want not only to call this evidence out of time, late in the case, but also you want to do it without calling the witness. We will grant you that indulgence but only if you agree that the Prosecution should have the same right in relation to the confidential witness"? What would your answer have been to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, discussing the question hypothetically in this way, what I can say is the following: I would never seek the Trial Chamber's indulgence for the Aleksovski case in overruling the protective measures from another case. I would never ask for that to happen. If something of that kind were to be asked by the opposite side, that is to say, by the Prosecution, and if the Trial Chamber were to grant that, then I would seek the possibility of appealing that decision because, quite frankly, I feel that there is no legal foundations and possibilities for something of that kind to take place. I don't know whether that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well then, you would have said, "I'm not prepared to pay that price." If you want to impose such a condition that you have to agree to this evidence of the confidential witness being admitted, you would then have called Admiral Domazet, would you, as a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to envisage a situation of that kind and I don't know what the confidential witness actually talked about, testified to.
